items.title: The middle income trap is real but not universal
items.claim: Many countries that reached middle income status (typically $4,000-$12,000 GDP per capita) have struggled to advance to high income. Which describes the phenomenon best?

options.text: A subset (Brazil, South Africa, Argentina, Thailand) have plateaued; others (South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, more recently Poland) have transitioned successfully. Drivers include education, institutional quality, R&D, and shifting from labour-intensive to knowledge-intensive production
All countries reach high income automatically

items.reveal:
The term was popularised by Indermit Gill and Homi Kharas's 2007 World Bank study. World Bank research (2013, 2018) found about 13 of 101 middle-income economies in 1960 reached high income by 2008.

South Korea's transition from low- to high-income was unusually rapid (1960-2000). It combined export orientation, investment in education and selective industrial policy. Argentina's reversal (from rich to middle income across the 20th century) shows the direction isn't fixed.
items.why: Development outcomes are heterogeneous. Single-factor explanations (geography, institutions, culture) often capture parts of the story but don't generalise.

items.title: FDI flows have plateaued since 2015
items.claim: Global Foreign Direct Investment flows reached record highs in the 2000s. UNCTAD data from 2020 onwards shows what pattern?

options.text: FDI flows have plateaued and partially fragmented along geopolitical lines (US-EU vs China-aligned blocs); 'slowbalisation' or 'fracturing globalisation' is the now-common framing
All FDI is now in the metaverse

items.reveal:
UNCTAD World Investment Report data: global FDI peaked at $2 trillion in 2015; 2022 flows were $1.3 trillion. Trade as a share of global GDP also flattened.

Drivers: US-China trade tensions (tariffs from 2018), COVID supply-chain reshoring, geopolitical fragmentation (Russia-Ukraine, Taiwan strait), reshoring/nearshoring policies (US CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act, IRA).

The 'end of history' globalisation narrative of the 1990s-2000s has been substantially complicated.
items.why: Globalisation is not a one-way ratchet. The political economy of trade and investment has shifted in ways that affect macroeconomic forecasting and corporate strategy.

items.title: The UK's 2010-2015 austerity programme
items.claim: The UK government under Osborne (2010-2016) pursued fiscal consolidation. What was the actual deficit reduction trajectory?

options.text: Budget deficit fell from ~10% of GDP (2009-10) to ~4% by 2015-16, but the target of eliminating it by 2015 was missed; growth was slower than OBR projections; public investment was cut sharply

items.reveal:
ONS data: UK fiscal deficit was 10.1% of GDP in 2009-10, 4.1% by 2015-16. The original 2010 emergency budget aimed to balance the structural deficit by 2015; the target was slipped repeatedly.

IFS and OBR analyses found growth fell short of pre-austerity forecasts. Economic historians (Blyth 'Austerity', 2013) and IMF research raised doubts about the timing of consolidation; defenders (Niemietz, others) argued the policy preserved fiscal credibility.

The austerity debate continues; the empirical record is contested but the speed of recovery was slower than baseline.
items.why: Major macroeconomic policy choices have decade-long effects that are hard to evaluate cleanly because counterfactuals are unobservable.
